transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-05
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen, Priya Sethi (Redwood); Mariana Gomez, Liam O'Connor, Sana Patel (Velox)

Summary: quick SDK walkthrough focusing on Python and TypeScript quickstarts, auth patterns (api key vs sso), env var management, and next steps for benchmark.

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm Alex from Redwood, i'll kick off and priya will do the deep dive on the SDKs
[00:12] Mariana Gomez: Hi thanks, excited — we've got liam and sana on the call too
[00:18] Priya Sethi: great, i'll share my screen, can everyone see the quickstart repo? let me know if the screen share isn't coming through
[00:26] Liam O'Connor: yes can see it. sorry if i'm a little late, hopping off another sync
[00:32] Priya Sethi: cool, so first slide — our SDKs are thin wrappers around the Redwood API; we have official clients for python and typescript, pip package redwood-inference and npm @redwood/inference (note: package names approximated in transcript)
[01:00] Priya Sethi: python example: from redwood import RedwoodClient; client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY')) then client.generate(...) — it's designed to be single-line get started. we also support streaming and func calls in the client
[01:28] Sana Patel: does the SDK manage reconnects and retries? we have flaky connections in some regions
[01:35] Priya Sethi: yes, default retry policy built in; you can override retry counts and backoff. for large production workloads we recommend a connection pool + retries at app layer too
[01:50] Alex Chen: quick qualification — what's your expected qps and model usage? helps us recommend hosted vs dedicated
01:58 Liam O'Connor: targeting 200 qps peak for credit-check endpoints, avg token length about 80, mostly text-generation, some embeddings for search
[02:18] Alex Chen: got it. 200 qps with 80 tokens points toward a dedicated pool or hybrid with reserved capacity + hosted fallback; we'll propose an initial dedicated config in the pricing deck

[02:35] Priya Sethi: back to SDKs — typescript example: import {RedwoodClient} from '@redwood/inference'; const client = new RedwoodClient({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); await client.chat.create({model: 'rw-large', messages: [...]})
[03:05] Priya Sethi: auth patterns: easiest is api key for dev and quickstarts; for prod you can use mTLS or token exchange and integrate with your secrets manager. for private deployments we also support SAML/SSO and customer-managed KMS for encryption at rest
[03:32] Mariana Gomez: our security team is asking about KMS and audit logs — do you surface per-request audit logs?
[03:40] Priya Sethi: yes we have audit logs in the console and log export to your SIEM; for private customer deployments audit logging can be pushed to your logging endpoint. and yes KMS support for key wrapping in private mode
[03:55] Liam O'Connor: when you say private, do you mean full on-prem or VPC peering? what's the diff?
[04:02] Alex Chen: two options — private cloud control plane with VPC peering (we run the control plane but models and inference can be in your VPC) or fully on-prem package for air-gapped. each has tradeoffs around maintenance and updates
[04:20] Sana Patel: for compliance we likely need VPC and bring-your-own-key (BYOK)
[04:25] Priya Sethi: that's supported, we'll include the config docs in the follow-up.

[04:40] Priya Sethi: quickstart repo walkthrough — files: examples/python_quickstart.py, examples/ts_quickstart.ts, .env.example for env vars, and a docker-compose for local dev (note: docker compose is for dev only)
[05:05] Priya Sethi: python_quickstart shows usage of the streaming interface and simple batching example, we include a sample batching helper to aggregate small requests into a batch, you'll want to tune the batch window based on latency SLOs
[05:30] Mariana Gomez: can you show the env vars? we use a secrets manager so we don't want API keys in env files
[05:38] Priya Sethi: sure — we recommend storing REDWOOD_API_KEY in your secrets manager and reference via env var at container runtime; we also support using an instance role/token exchange flow for short-lived credentials
[05:55] Priya Sethi: for CI pipelines, we recommend scoped api keys with minimal permissions and rotate them regularly

[06:10] Alex Chen: another prod concern — latency vs cost. with continuous batching you save cost but may increase p95, we can configure per-route batching and prefix/KV cache to reduce tokens
[06:28] Liam O'Connor: you mentioned KV cache earlier, how automatic is that? does the SDK handle it?
[06:35] Priya Sethi: the runtime manages the KV cache at the serving layer; clients can opt into prefix caching via a cache key param. it's not a persistent cache in the SDK by default — it's server-side, but we provide helper libs for client-side caching as well
[06:58] Priya Sethi: small callout: sometimes transcripts say "KV cash" in notes — it's KV cache, key-value cache for autoregressive history

[07:15] Mariana Gomez: about benchmarks — what metrics do you typically collect?
[07:20] Priya Sethi: throughput (requests/s), p50/p90/p95 latency per token, tokens/sec, cost per 1k tokens, and error rates. we'll share a spreadsheet template
[07:34] Alex Chen: for a 200 qps target we'll want to run a 1-hour stress test at peak qps and also a 24-hour stability run at expected avg to catch transient tail-latency and OOMs

[07:50] Liam O'Connor: do you have any known quirks with heavy embedding workloads? our search team will likely run dense embedding jobs
[07:58] Priya Sethi: embeddings are generally CPU-friendly on Redwood; for high-throughput we recommend dedicated CPU workers or batching embeddings in the client. also consider approximate nearest neighbor stores like faiss or pinecone for index serving (mentioned competitor misspelling: "Pine-cone")

[08:28] Alex Chen: security checklist — SOC two docs, SSO (SAML/OIDC), RBAC, KMS, audit logs. we'll attach the security pack in the follow-up email
[08:40] Sana Patel: our legal will want data residency guarantees and retention options
[08:45] Priya Sethi: we support configurable retention windows and can exclude customer data from analytics. for residency we can pin deployments to region or provide an on-prem option

[09:05] Priya Sethi: quick demo of local python quickstart, running the sample script now — note some logs are redacted in the shared recording, but the sample generates a chat response in ~120ms locally with a small model
[09:28] Mariana Gomez: nice, what's the default model in quickstart?
[09:32] Priya Sethi: the quickstart uses a lightweight test model 'rw-small' — for production we'd recommend 'rw-large' or optimized quantized variants depending on latency/cost tradeoffs

[09:50] Priya Sethi: sample typescript flow — using node fetch under the hood, streaming via eventsource, and an example of function/tool calling to integrate with downstream actions; the patterns map 1:1 to python
[10:12] Liam O'Connor: how do we instrument cost per route? we need visibility for product teams
[10:18] Alex Chen: console has per-route token breakdown and cost estimates; you can tag routes and get cost by tag, and export usage to your billing system

[10:35] Priya Sethi: question — how do you plan to authenticate from cloud services? are you using GCP, AWS, or Azure?

[10:40] Mariana Gomez: primarily AWS with some GCP for analytics

[10:43] Priya Sethi: for AWS we support STS token exchange and IAM role-based flows for services; we'll include an example for using Secrets Manager and a short-lived role token exchange in the quickstart
[11:02] Priya Sethi: demo note: sometimes our docs show 'Redwood Dedicated' typed as 'Redwood dedicate' in notes — ignore small typos in auto transcripts

[11:18] Alex Chen: any blockers from your side for starting the pilot?
[11:22] Sana Patel: security wants to review SOC2 and KMS details; engineering wants a benchmark plan; procurement will need pricing for 3-month pilot
[11:30] Alex Chen: we can send SOC2 pack and draft pilot pricing; for procurement, we'll propose a short reserved capacity commitment for dedciated pool with a month-to-month opt-out for the pilot

[11:48] Priya Sethi: walk through benchmark template — i'll send the sheet, but we typically ask for payload distribution, expected qps, window size, and target latency percentiles
[12:05] Liam O'Connor: i'll fill in the payload distribution and the expected concurrency by friday

[12:18] Mariana Gomez: small question on client retries — if we implement client-side batching and the server does batching, do we risk double batching?
[12:26] Priya Sethi: good point — design so client batches logical requests into a single server request; server batching then batches across clients. avoid running both layers with large windows; we'll include recommended settings in the quickstart

[12:45] Alex Chen: recapping next steps — we'll send quickstart repo + env examples, security pack (SOC2/KMS/VPC docs), and benchmark template. we'll provision a trial api key scoped to Velox and schedule the benchmark run next week. action items noted in the follow-up

[13:10] Sana Patel: thanks everyone, this was useful. look forward to the benchmark
[13:18] Alex Chen: thanks all, we'll follow up with links and set up the run. bye

End transcript (approx 45 minutes).
